People ask me every week which city they should choose, and I always give the same answer. If you have four days, go to Dubrovnik, because the walls are the most impressive thing on this coast and you should see them once in your life. But go in the morning. By noon the main street is more crowded than any place I know, and it becomes exhausting rather than beautiful. If you have ten days, add Ljubljana. It is quieter, greener and much cheaper, and honestly it is the most underrated capital in this part of Europe. The two cities are not competing. They are simply good at different things.

Welcome back to the tour. Look at the two buildings in front of you. The one on the left is older, but the one on the right is better preserved, and that is not an accident. The building on the right was restored twice, once after the earthquake and again in the nineteen nineties. The one on the left kept its original stone, so it is more authentic, but it is also far more fragile. Which is better? Architects argue about this everywhere in Europe. The most honest answer is that a city needs both: the building you restore, and the building you leave alone.

First she arrived in Dubrovnik and walked the walls at seven in the morning, when the stone was completely empty. By eleven the main street was more crowded than she expected, so she left the old town. Then she took the slower road north and arrived in Ljubljana in the evening. She crossed the whole centre on foot in twenty minutes and could not believe how compact it was. In the end she decided that the two cities are simply good at different things.
